conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short tool called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless safety requires otherwise. I’ll read each question aloud; just tell me what feels closest to your experience. Ready to begin?

1. Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has that happened as much as it used to, a little less, almost never, or definitely not at all?

[soft half-smile]  
It’s… not quite the same. I still laugh sometimes—like if my partner pulls a goofy face—but it feels a little less bright, like the volume’s turned down. I’d say “a little less.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can still laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as bright as it used to—so I’d say “a little less.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs gently, eyes on the floor for a sec]  
I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when the baby finally naps so I can breathe—but the excitement feels kind of muted. I’d say “a little less.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet laugh, embarrassed]  
Yeah… if the baby’s fussy or I can’t settle her right away, I hear myself thinking, “You’re not doing this right, you’re failing at the one job you have.” It’s not constant—just sometimes—but it’s definitely there. So I’d tick “yes, some of the time.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes my heart just races out of nowhere, like I’m bracing for something bad to happen even when everything’s quiet. It’s not all day, but it keeps popping up. I’d say “yes, some of the time.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Every now and then I’ll be feeding her and suddenly feel this wave of “what-if-something-awful-happens” wash over me. My chest gets tight and I have to remind myself to breathe. It’s not every day, but it’s happened a couple of times this week, so—“yes, some of the time.”
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath]  
There’ve been moments—like when she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up—when everything feels stacked too high. I usually get through it, but yesterday I had to set her in the crib for five minutes and step outside just to clear my head. So I’d say “yes, some of the time I haven’t coped as well as usual.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, thankfully I haven’t been that unhappy. I do have nights where it takes me a while to fall asleep, but it’s more from buzzing thoughts than from feeling really low, so I’d tick “not at all.”
I have felt sad or miserable

[purses lips, shrugs a little]  
Yeah, a couple of evenings this week I just felt… flat and weepy, like a cloud parked over me. It passes, but it’s definitely been there, so I’d say “yes, some of the time.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quick, sheepish nod]  
Twice—once when she wouldn’t latch and once when my partner found me staring at the mess in the kitchen. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears when I felt overwhelmed, so “yes, some of the time.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that over the past week moments of joy feel dimmer, worries and sudden panic arise while caring for your baby, and you sometimes blame yourself when things go wrong, yet you remain hopeful and firmly deny any thoughts of self-harm; these mixed emotions are common in new motherhood and your honesty helps us understand how best to support you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly identifies with "yes, some of the time" and describes specific self-blame when baby is fussy.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, unexplained surges of anxiety/racing heart that occur "sometimes," clearly aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of fear/tight chest while feeding baby, occurring "some of the time" this week, aligning with "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific moments of overwhelm and needing to step away, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports clear sadness lasting "a couple of evenings this week" and "some of the time", matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 13 places you above the cutoff where <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety disorders</med> become likely; your descriptions of <sym>muted enjoyment</sym>, frequent <sym>racing heart</sym>, <sym>what-if catastrophizing</sym>, and needing to step away when tasks pile up align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Because you still laugh, sleep reasonably, and care for your baby safely, symptoms are moderate but warrant prompt follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within one week
2. Continue open conversations; call a support line or 988 if distress escalates
3. Involve trusted family or friends for practical help and emotional backup
4. Use five-minute breathing breaks when overwhelmed; place baby in a safe spot first
5. Keep a brief mood log to track patterns for your next visit
6. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___________  Gestational/PP weeks: ___________  Infant age: ___________

Patient-reported symptoms (EPDS-10 paraphrase):
- Anhedonia: diminished capacity for laughter and anticipatory enjoyment (“a little less”)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame “some of the time” when infant is fussy
- Anxiety: episodic racing heart, “what-if” catastrophizing, chest tightness “some of the time”
- Panic-like surges twice this week without clear trigger
- Feeling overwhelmed and inadequately coping “some of the time”; needed to set infant down and step away
- Sad/miserable and tearful episodes “some of the time” (two crying spells reported)
- Sleep onset delay related to racing thoughts, not severe mood-related insomnia
- Denies any self-harm ideation

Pattern: sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging several times per week, with preserved infant attachment and no safety concerns.

Screening significance
- EPDS items 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 endorsed at “some of the time” level → total provisional score 6–7 (above conventional cutoff for further assessment)
- Risk factors: primiparous adjustment, self-criticism, anxiety-driven avoidance (stepping away), intermittent crying
- Protective factors: denies anhedonia entirely, denies self-harm, able to implement coping (setting infant safely, partner support noted)

Clinical observation
Meets screening criteria for possible postpartum anxiety with mild depressive features; not acute but warrants formal evaluation with standardized tool (EPDS full scoring) and clinician interview to clarify diagnosis and inform level-of-care decision.

Safety: no suicidal or infanticidal ideation elicited; no immediate safety concerns identified at this time.

Next steps: review score, schedule follow-up within 1 week; provide psycho-education handout; encourage support system activation; discuss further assessment/treatment options.
